paragraphs: The Alaska Senate race between Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola was still too close to call Wednesday evening, according to the Washington Examiner. Peltola led 102,701 to 102,075 in first-choice votes, a 626-vote edge, with an estimated 74% of votes counted. The Associated Press has not called the race.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting. If no candidate wins more than 50% of first-choice votes, the last-place candidate is eliminated and those ballots transfer to each voter's next choice, repeating until someone holds a majority. Sullivan's campaign argues in a memo that enough voters who backed the two trailing candidates ranked him next to put him ahead. Using available ballot data, it projected a 105,037 to 104,709 win. That figure is the campaign's own projection.

A legal fight sits alongside the count. The Justice Department filed a civil complaint on Oct. 22 seeking to block certification if Sullivan lost but would have won had votes for Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a spoiler candidate with the same name who has more than 3,500 votes, gone to him instead. Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the suit Sunday, finding no workable remedy that preserved ballot secrecy. The department appealed to the 9th Circuit, where its opening brief is due Dec. 14 and a response Jan. 11, 2027. Attorney General Todd Blanche defended preserving ballots, saying Sullivan "could lose, but really he didn't lose" if confusion affected the outcome.

A separate criminal investigation has reportedly produced more than 120 subpoenas. The DOJ also sent more than 20 target and document preservation letters, including to Democratic lawyer Marc Elias, whose firm has represented Peltola's campaign; whether he is a target is unclear. The inquiry follows an Oct. 28 New York Times report that Democratic operatives linked to Peltola's campaign helped recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. Peltola's campaign has denied involvement. Blanche declined to confirm the letters.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., formally announced Wednesday that he is running for Speaker in the next Congress, according to Fox News. In a letter to House Democrats he wrote that he "humbly" requests their support. Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar, his top deputies, signaled they would seek the No. 2 and No. 3 positions. House Democrats are scheduled to hold leadership elections in mid-December.

Fox reported that Democrats were projected to win 237 seats to the GOP's 139, with 59 races still too close to call. Jeffries told reporters he expects Democrats to hold at least 255 seats. Fox said he will likely win the gavel easily given that margin, though it noted a small group of far-left members could pose difficulties. Al Jazeera reported he is set to become the first Black Speaker when the new Congress convenes in January.

Jeffries called the result "an American tsunami" and said Democrats "ran on affordability" and now must govern on it. In his letter he pledged to seek bipartisan common ground where possible while criticizing Trump tariffs and the war in Iran, which he said raised costs. He said the House would act as a check on the executive branch, and suggested Democrats would try to undo Republican Medicaid cuts, extend expired enhanced Obamacare tax credits and end the Iran war. He said Democrats would follow the facts and law on administration accountability, and that Americans want results rather than to "get even."

Al Jazeera noted that President Trump has threatened vetoes, which could make it hard for Democrats to pass new laws even with a majority. On the Republican side, Fox reported that Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise are expected to compete for minority leader.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Wednesday he expects to be chosen majority leader in the next Congress, even though some incoming Democratic senators oppose him, Fox News reported. After declining at first to address the question, Schumer said, "the issue is not me. I'll be re-elected as majority leader."

To win the post, Schumer needs a simple majority of the Senate Democratic caucus in a closed-door vote. According to Fox, no sitting Democratic senator has publicly said they will oppose him, but five newly elected senators have: Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Julia Stratton of Illinois, Troy Jackson of Maine, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan. James Talarico of Texas has not said how he will vote. Fox said five votes would not be enough to sink Schumer and that no one else has sought the job. The page text did not include Indivisible's statement calling for his replacement.

Schumer described the election as "a generational remake of the Senate map." He said voters did not hand Democrats the majority "so we can do whatever we want," and that Republicans "squandered" their own opportunity two years ago. He said voters want lower living costs and action on government corruption, and named ending the Iran war, which he linked to elevated energy prices, as a priority.

Schumer also said the Senate will launch investigations of President Trump whenever he "defies the will of the American people or the law." He initially resisted questions about whether he would be open to getting rid of the filibuster. The leadership vote is the next point to watch.

Two U.S. airmen died last week in what the Pentagon classifies as non-hostile incidents amid the war in Iran, bringing the number of American fatalities since the war began to 23, Defense News reported. Their deaths appear in the Pentagon's Defense Casualty Analysis System, which lists one as illness- or injury-related and the other as pending.

An Air Force spokesperson said one airman was active duty and the other was in the Air National Guard. One died in the area covered by U.S. Central Command; the other died in the United States. The spokesperson declined to say where the second airman had been operating or how they were transported home. The pending death is under investigation, but the spokesperson did not say which department is conducting it. Both were mid- to senior-enlisted personnel, and the Air Force has not released their names, though Defense Department policy typically calls for names to be made public 24 hours after next of kin are notified. The spokesperson declined to say why.

The casualty system lists both deaths under an Overseas Operations category rather than Operation Epic Fury. A Pentagon official said that is because the U.S. considers Epic Fury concluded; a defense official previously gave May 5 as the end date. Overseas Operations lists a July 7 start. Democratic members of Congress have criticized the classification, accusing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth of trying to hide casualties.

Overseas Operations now includes eight deaths, four hostile and four non-hostile, while Epic Fury lists 15. The war began Feb. 28. Across both categories, 866 service members have been wounded in action, 417 under Epic Fury and 449 under Overseas Operations, according to the system.

Democratic wins in both chambers of Congress could reshape Pentagon spending and oversight, according to Breaking Defense and Defense One. Breaking Defense said several veteran defense lawmakers are leaving and the lame-duck session will include major decisions on defense funding and a possible reconciliation package. It also said renewed efforts to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could force House Republicans into a politically difficult vote.

Defense One reported that costly initiatives such as Golden Dome, Golden Fleet and Autonomous Warfare Command could lose funding. Todd Harrison of the American Enterprise Institute told the outlet that anything requiring new funding is likely to "hit a brick wall," calling the Golden Fleet, especially its battleship, a "dead idea." He said the administration may still pursue changes it can make alone, and that Congress could try to reverse them by law. Mark Cancian of the Center for Strategic and International Studies said that if a reconciliation bill is dropped, the administration's $1.5 trillion defense proposal would shrink to a still substantial $1.1 trillion. He noted that drones, munitions, shipbuilding and missile defense have bipartisan support.

On Hegseth, Harrison said nearly all Democrats and a growing number of Republicans want him removed, though he did not think the votes exist to remove him in the Senate. An impeachment vote with Republican support might still embarrass the administration enough to push him out, he said. Trump told reporters Wednesday that Hegseth is "doing a very good job." Defense One also noted rumors that Hegseth wants to fill Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn's Senate seat; Trump said he had not heard that.
Harrison said the lame-duck period is the window to replace a secretary and still win confirmation, since the new Congress may struggle to confirm anyone.

House Democrats plan to investigate how Trump administration cuts to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency affected its ability to protect federal networks and help states secure elections, Defense One reported. Senate Democrats, meanwhile, say they will examine whether intelligence agencies can deliver findings that contradict the president without putting analysts' jobs at risk. With majorities in both chambers from January, Democrats will control subpoenas and confirmation hearings.

Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., in line to chair the House Homeland Security Committee, said the panel will look at the department's use of its powers against Americans, immigration enforcement and contractor dealings. He told Nextgov/FCW, "We will investigate the administration weaponizing DHS against Americans." Thompson and Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., have asked Congress's watchdog to assess the impact of CISA staffing cuts. The agency lost roughly a third of its workforce after Trump returned to office. Acting Director Nick Andersen said that by September about 250 prospective hires had tentative offers pending clearances. The administration's response to the investigation plans was not reported.
One deadline falls before Democrats take over: a law protecting companies from lawsuits when they share cyber threat information is operating under a temporary extension through Dec. 11.

On intelligence, Rep. Jim Himes and Sen. Mark Warner are in line to chair their chambers' intelligence committees. Defense One pointed to disputes over an assessment of the Tren de Aragua gang, after which then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard fired the two leaders of the National Intelligence Council, and over Iran's nuclear program. Warner has accused the administration of "treating intelligence as a loyalty test."

Voters backed restrictions on data centers in most places where they were on the ballot, Ars Technica reported. Citing the polling firm Redbud Consulting, it said 38 of 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers have passed so far, including moratoriums and bans. Analysts suggested these would mostly affect projects planned for 2028, not those already under construction or approved through 2027. One measure that allowed a data center to proceed, in a North Dakota city, still required developers to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings.

Gubernatorial results added to the pressure. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won in Texas, which Axios said was expected to account for more than 41 percent of added data center capacity in 2028. According to Bloomberg, she plans to delay projects until laws address water, electricity, air and property rights, exposing roughly 13 gigawatts of capacity. Democrats also won governor races in Arizona, Georgia and Ohio. Axios projected nearly two-thirds of 2028 capacity could face delays.

Interpretations differ. Adam Kovacevich of the industry group Chamber of Progress said the results show "little evidence of a voter mandate to crack down on AI or data centers," noting Democratic gubernatorial candidates who opposed data center bans won at a higher rate than those who backed them. He urged people not to "confuse an anti-Trump wave with an anti-tech mandate."

Alejandra Montoya-Boyer of The Leadership Conference's Center for Civil Rights and Technology disagreed, calling the midterms the first true AI election. She cited NBC polling that she said showed 3 in 4 voters oppose data centers and more than half saw AI and data centers as a crucial or major factor in their vote. NBC exit polls also showed cost of living and corruption ranked as more significant issues.

Leading the Future, the largest pro-AI super PAC network, ended the midterms with just over $20 million in the bank and a list of successful candidates, but Wired reported its influence appears limited. The network launched in August 2025 with about $100 million from backers including Andreessen Horowitz, Joe Lonsdale and Greg Brockman. Wired said its donations went overwhelmingly to safe candidates and that its involvement in riskier races mostly fell flat. Leading the Future did not respond to Wired's requests for comment.

The group spent about $26 million in independent expenditures in primaries, including millions on attack ads against Democrat Alex Bores in New York's 12th district. Bores, who ran on an AI safety platform, finished second to Micah Lasher after the Anthropic-backed network Public First spent $15 million supporting him. In the general election the network spent about $10 million and reported no donations in the second and third quarters. Sacha Haworth of the Tech Oversight Project called the later spending an attempt to ingratiate itself with incoming members.

Results in competitive races were mixed. Wired reported Darline Graham, who received more than $2 million from the network's American Mission PAC, lost in South Carolina with 46.5 percent. Democrat Jared Moskowitz, backed through Think Big, won by 13,000 votes. In North Carolina's 1st district, its preferred Republican primary candidate, Laurie Buckhout, lost the general election to Democrat Don Davis. In Montana, backed candidate Aaron Flint conceded to Democrat Sam Forstag, though the Associated Press had not called the race.

Brad Carson of Public First Action called the results a "crushing blow" to the AI industry's anti-regulatory efforts. An NBC exit poll found 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers played a major role in their vote.

A New York state appeals court has cleared the way for Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration to keep implementing an annual surcharge on high-value second homes, the Washington Examiner reported. The panel overturned a September ruling by a Staten Island judge that had sided with homeowners challenging the rollout.

The appeals court found that the plaintiffs lacked standing because they had not shown that the tax or the publication of property information caused them a concrete injury. "The petitioners did not allege for injury purposes that any bad actors have misused the information purveyed by the supplemental roll, or that the publication itself subjected them to any crime, harassment, or defined public ridicule," the judges wrote. The panel added that publishing the supplemental property roll did not create a legal obligation or alter the homeowners' rights.

The plaintiffs were represented by Randy Mastro, a former first deputy mayor under Eric Adams. They argued that city officials wrongly flagged primary residences, did not make individualized determinations before sending notices, and shifted the burden to homeowners to prove they qualified for exemptions. The city had published a list identifying more than 960,000 homeowners whose properties could potentially be subject to the surcharge. Judge Wayne Ozzi twice ordered the rollout halted, but the appeals court stayed both decisions. The deadline to apply for exemptions was Oct. 13.

Under the tax, houses valued above $5 million would pay annual rates of 0.8% to 1.3%, while condominiums and co-ops above $1 million would pay 4% to 6.5%. Supporters estimate it could raise $500 million a year.

Mamdani said those with the most had tried "every legal avenue" to avoid contributing, and that the ruling rejected an attempt by the ultrawealthy to avoid paying their fair share. The plaintiffs' response was not reported. The decision does not resolve two separate constitutional challenges, including one by Wilbur Ross and Steve Wynn arguing the surcharge discriminates against people who do not live in the city. Those cases go to court on Dec. 1.

Two people were killed, including the gunman, in a shooting at a Citibank office campus in Brandon, Florida, about 15 miles from Tampa, on Wednesday, according to the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office. The shooting began shortly after noon, when about 3,200 people were working at the site.

Chief Deputy Frank Losat said the suspect drove a vehicle through a fence and into a courtyard where employees were eating lunch, then opened fire with a rifle and killed a woman. An armed security guard confronted the gunman in the cafeteria and the two exchanged fire. The guard fatally shot the suspect, authorities said. The suspect was taken to a hospital, where he later died, Losat said. Four other people were hospitalized with injuries not considered life-threatening.
"Was there a potential for further violence? Absolutely," Losat said. "So kudos to that security guard."

More than 300 deputies and officers responded. Losat said the first patrol unit arrived about a minute after emergency calls began around 12:11 p.m. The campus has four three-story office buildings, and authorities spent roughly 2.5 hours searching the complex to make sure there were no other threats.

Losat did not identify the suspect, the victim or the security guard. Investigators were working to determine a motive and whether the suspect had any connection to the victim or the campus. Citigroup confirmed the incident in a statement, saying it was coordinating with law enforcement. Footage showed employees evacuating, and hundreds of workers sheltered at nearby hotels while deputies set up a reunification site for employees and families at a Tampa East hotel.

Search teams in British Columbia have found the body of a 20-year-old woman and confirmed that she and her mother were killed in an attack near their home, according to The Guardian and the BBC. Both outlets describe it as a suspected grizzly bear attack. Conservation officers said more than one bear may have been involved.

The women were identified as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20. Their family reported them missing on Nov. 1 when they did not return from what was meant to be a short afternoon walk. Their vehicle was found at a trailhead near Bella Coola. Balcarras's remains were found Monday and Reed's on Tuesday, during searches by conservation officers and the RCMP. The area is the Snooka West trail, about 8 km east of Bella Coola.

Inspector Jeff Tyre of the BC Conservation Officer Service said evidence at the scene suggested an animal may have been involved, and the service was investigating whether more than one bear was responsible. He asked the public to stay out of the area. He said any captured bear would be assessed and, if found to have been involved, would be killed under provincial human-wildlife conflict guidelines.

The community was already shaken. Last November a grizzly attacked a school group near the Nuxalk community of 4 Mile, injuring 11 people, and that bear was never found. Nuxalk Nation chief Samuel Schooner said a trapping effort was under way.
Relatives described Balcarras, an art therapist who had recently moved to Bella Coola for a new job, and Reed as very close. A family fundraiser is helping with funeral costs.

Commonwealth leaders say the United Kingdom has agreed to "structured dialogue" over the next year with Caribbean nations affected by the slave trade and its legacy, The Guardian reported. Antigua and Barbuda's prime minister, Gaston Browne, said the Commonwealth heads of government meeting reached a "consensus" on a way forward.

Browne said he hoped the dialogue would take place within 12 months, and that governments had agreed in principle to set up its framework by the end of this year or early next year. He praised UK prime minister Andy Burnham for showing "courage and goodwill" and said the region would not make "unreasonable demands."

Burnham announced on Friday that he wanted to begin the dialogue and was open to Britain apologising, but ruled out reparations. He proposed talks on debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations and announced £40m for critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over three years. Browne said the Caribbean position was that reparations must be part of the dialogue.

Others argue that aid is not a substitute. A 10-point plan from the Caribbean Community's reparations commission asks for debt cancellation, not restructuring, and monetary compensation. Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines, said many of the items Burnham and the king mentioned appear in the plan but also fall under UN development goals, and that such assistance remains at the UK's discretion.
Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy said reparative justice must be made with those affected, or it is not reparations. The UK government's response to these criticisms was not included in the report.

A run of intense and sometimes unpredictable storms, worsened by El Niño, has killed dozens, closed major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across East Asia in recent months, the BBC reports.

In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as Typhoon Champi, with winds of 295 km/h, approached. It did not make landfall but brought heavy rain, and hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. Earlier, two storms heading for Japan in June forced one million people to evacuate. In August, Super Typhoon Dolphin hit eastern China after 16 days over the Pacific, causing floods and dozens of casualties.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern that recurs every two to seven years. The UK Met Office has forecast this one to be the "strongest in living memory," lasting until February or March. The BBC says storm energy for the region is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average, and typhoons are forming farther east and strengthening over warm water. Last month, equatorial Pacific sea surface temperatures were 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency. China's climate agency expects temperatures to keep rising for three months.
Philippine climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated warmer conditions on past storms and found accumulated rainfall rose 26%.

Countries are preparing. Japan has urged residents to stockpile supplies, China is upgrading warning systems, and the Philippines and neighbors are supporting farmers to protect rice. The UN Development Programme says the window for governments to act is "closing."

Researchers have found hundreds of engraved motifs and dozens of animal images in a Spanish cave that had gone unnoticed despite being a popular tourist attraction, New Scientist reports. The site is Cova de la Font Major, west of Barcelona.

Josep Maria Vergès of the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology came across the art after noticing a tourist group in wetsuits emerging from a side gallery. Inside, he saw walls covered in modern names and dates carved since 1957. He then lit the wall with raking light, a technique that casts shadows in incised grooves, and noticed vertical lines that looked ancient. Turning to the opposite wall, he saw a horse in what he recognized as a Palaeolithic style.
So far, 280 motifs have been found in the gallery, including 55 animal figures. The report calls it one of the richest archaeological finds along the Iberian coast between the Pyrenees and Gibraltar.
Dating the engravings themselves is very difficult. Human occupation of the cave has been dated to between 26,000 and 41,000 years ago, and based on style the art is likely over 19,000 years old.

Team member Míriam Salas-Altès highlighted a hind with its head lowered, its muzzle across a natural crack that may have been used to represent water. She said that, if correct, it would be one of the earliest known depictions of water in human art. Non-figurative marks include grouped lines and series of up to 40 parallel lines.
Paul Taçon of Griffith University said the find fills a large gap in knowledge of Palaeolithic art distribution in western Europe, though the exact age is still undetermined.

The US Court of Federal Claims has ruled that the Navy unfairly evaluated Saildrone's proposal for its medium unmanned surface vessel program, according to Breaking Defense. Judge Philip Hadji wrote that the Navy engaged in disparate treatment and acted in an arbitrary and capricious manner. The opinion was issued Oct. 30 and made public Wednesday.

The Navy had barred Saildrone from on-water testing because its summary document, known as a Placemat, reported loaded displacements above the stated maximum. The court found the Navy advanced a proposal from Sea Machines despite similar displacement issues, either reporting displacements above the maximum or leaving the fields blank, thereby holding Saildrone to a higher standard.

The court ordered the Navy to reevaluate Saildrone's proposal within 60 days using the approach applied to firms that advanced. It also barred the Navy from spending more than $1.5 billion of the program's $2.1 billion on production until the reevaluation is complete. A Navy spokesperson said it will comply. Saildrone CEO Richard Jenkins called the ruling a win for fair competition, taxpayers and national security.

The court reached a different conclusion on Blue Water Autonomy, finding the Navy reasonably rated it unacceptable. The Navy had said the company's catamaran test vessel was not representative of its monohull production vessel. The court held that "representative" unambiguously calls for comparing the two. Blue Water's Austin Gray said nothing about the test vessel was core to its technology.

Gray noted the Navy's Phase II, unveiled in September, requires two 20-foot containers and drops the high-speed requirement. Navy official Christopher Miller said the service wants to "open the aperture" for new entrants.

A record number of federal candidates backed by or affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America won in Tuesday's midterms, according to Al Jazeera. DSA electoral commission member Chanpreet Singh called it a record for the group. The outlet says the movement has more than 120,000 members, with chapters in all 50 states.

Al Jazeera lists wins in New York, where Claire Valdez, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Brad Lander were elected to the House for the first time and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was re-elected. In Michigan, Rashida Tlaib was re-elected and Donavan McKinney won a House seat. Melat Kiros won in Colorado, Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, and Angela Gonzales-Torres unseated a Democratic incumbent in Los Angeles. Adam Hamawy won in New Jersey; he is not a DSA member but has aligned with the movement.

Fox News reported a setback in California. The DSA backed Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on billionaires, which the secretary of state's results showed heading for defeat as of Wednesday afternoon. The DSA argued it would help cover a projected $100 billion shortfall in federal funding for Medi-Cal, with 90% of revenue going to healthcare.

Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed it, calling it "a badly written initiative" and noting opposition from firefighters, teachers and Planned Parenthood. He backed Proposition 42, which would bar new state taxes on personal property, and which Fox said appeared on track to pass. Newsom said a national version might be a different conversation.
Richard Stern of Advancing American Freedom told Fox that billionaires' wealth is mostly business assets, not cash. The DSA's response to the results was not reported.

Sen. Ted Cruz, a Texas Republican, is moving to widen the Republican majority on the Federal Communications Commission before Democrats take control of the Senate in January 2027, Ars Technica reported. Cruz announced a Nov. 10 nomination hearing for Danielle Thumann Severs, President Trump's FCC nominee, in his last two months as chairman of the Commerce Committee.

Thumann Severs is an attorney and senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Her confirmation would give Republicans a 3-1 edge. That could become 3-0 at the end of 2027, when Democrat Anna Gomez must leave unless Trump renominates her. Cruz's office had not responded to questions about a confirmation vote.

Federal law requires three commissioners for a quorum and limits how many may belong to one party to a bare majority of the commission. Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, wrote in a September letter that an all-Republican FCC would be prohibited and its actions could be overturned in court. He said there was speculation that Trump intends to fire Gomez after confirmation to run a 3-0 panel.

By tradition, presidents nominate opposing-party commissioners on recommendations from that party's Senate leaders, often paired with their own nominees. Trump has not nominated a Democrat to the other empty seat or renominated Gomez. Twenty-one Democrats on the House Commerce Committee wrote to Cruz and Senate Majority Leader John Thune urging that any new Republican nominee be paired with a Democrat, including Gomez.

Gomez issued a statement urging Congress to fill the vacancies in a bipartisan way. Her term technically expired June 30, but she may serve until the end of 2027 or until a replacement is confirmed. Thumann Severs would fill a different seat, with a term ending in 2029.

Qualcomm reported quarterly results on Wednesday that topped Wall Street estimates, but its earnings forecast came in lighter than expected, according to CNBC. The stock slid 7% in extended trading. For the current quarter, Qualcomm said it expects earnings per share of $2.15 to $2.35 on revenue of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion. Analysts had expected $2.27 per share on revenue of $10.48 billion.

Most of Qualcomm's chip sales are smartphone chips and modems, a market CNBC described as in turmoil because rising memory costs are forcing handset makers to raise prices and hurting demand. Handset chip sales fell 26% to $5.14 billion, below a StreetAccount estimate of $5.21 billion, even after Qualcomm raised prices in September. The company said Android shipments in China have bottomed and that it is seeing sequential growth, though it expects the handset market to be flat in 2027. CEO Cristiano Amon said: "We don't have a demand issue; it's a supply issue."

Qualcomm is trying to shift investor attention to AI data center chips. CNBC reported $650 million in data center revenue in the quarter, mostly from customizing and connectivity work, and Amon said he expects $5 billion in fiscal 2027. The Verge, which cited partnerships with Amazon and Meta announced earlier this year, described the $650 million as a forecast for the first quarter of 2027. It also reported targets of $15 billion by 2029 and data centers eventually making up about 30% of the business.

Elsewhere, automotive revenue rose 89% to $1.99 billion, and Internet of things revenue rose 4% to $1.88 billion. Licensing revenue fell 7% to $1.3 billion, and Qualcomm said it renewed licensing agreements with Apple, Huawei and Transsion. Earlier Wednesday it announced a deal to provide technology for SpaceX's cellular buildout.

Snap shares fell sharply after the Snapchat parent missed analyst expectations on revenue and daily active users in its third-quarter report on Wednesday. CNBC put the drop at more than 10%, while TechCrunch reported 12%. Snap reported 495 million daily active users, up from 493 million in the previous quarter but short of the 499 million analysts expected, according to TechCrunch.

CNBC reported that sales rose 14% from a year earlier and that Snap posted net income of $56 million, compared with a $104 million net loss a year before. Adjusted earnings were $383 million, above the $337 million analysts projected, according to StreetAccount. For the fourth quarter, Snap forecast revenue of $1.95 billion to $1.99 billion, with a midpoint above Wall Street's $1.95 billion estimate, and adjusted earnings of $490 million to $525 million against an expected $498 million.

Snap said that starting in the first quarter of 2027, global monthly active users will become its primary audience metric. An investor letter said the company does not intend to optimize Snapchat around daily use at the expense of long-term value. Chief commercial officer Ronan Harris told analysts that lower spending by consumer packaged goods companies hurt sales, which he attributed to macro pressures in the U.S. and the Middle East. He said Snap is seeing growth in other areas such as financial services in the U.S.

Separately, Snap said it has passed 30 million paid subscribers across Snapchat+, Memories Storage and Lens+, up 5 million since February, according to TechCrunch. CEO Evan Spiegel said paid subscribers are still a small share of the monthly community. He also said advertising revenue growth remains below the company's target and that Snap plans to prioritize improving advertiser performance and expanding the ways businesses can reach users.

AMD reported record third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45 percent from a year earlier, according to Ars Technica. The growth was driven by the data center business, which nearly doubled, while the gaming segment fell sharply.

Data center revenue rose 97 percent to a record $8.5 billion. AMD attributed this to demand for its EPYC server CPUs and the launch of its Instinct MI450 series GPUs. Operating margin in the segment rose from 25 percent to 34 percent, with operating income up 168 percent to $2.88 billion. CEO Lisa Su said AMD started shipping MI455X in volume during the quarter and that lead customers including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle brought their first Helios racks online quickly.

The Client segment brought in $2.95 billion, up 7 percent, led by Ryzen mobile chips. Embedded revenue was $1.1 billion, up 29 percent. Gaming revenue fell 40 percent to $773 million. Su attributed the decline primarily to lower semi-custom sales, as expected at this stage of the console cycle. Ars Technica noted the results do not split console chip sales from PC graphics cards.

For the fourth quarter, CFO Jean Hu said AMD expects revenue of about $17 billion, plus or minus 3 percent, roughly 66 percent growth from a year earlier. Citing Tom's Hardware, Ars Technica said Intel's fourth-quarter guidance is $15 billion to $16 billion, so AMD would exceed Intel's revenue for the first time if both land as expected.

AMD also highlighted upcoming hardware, including the Threadripper Halo Station, due sometime in 2027 with pricing to be announced, and Windows-based systems on its Ryzen AI Halo platform, which it said are coming soon.

Meta has acquired Conductor, an AI coding startup whose software lets users start software projects by deploying multiple AI agents into parallel workspaces, TechCrunch reported. Axios first reported the news, and Conductor announced it on its blog. Meta confirmed the acquisition to TechCrunch but declined to comment further or provide details, so the terms of the deal were not disclosed.

Founder and CEO Charlie Holtz wrote on Wednesday that Conductor is joining Meta. He said the company has "big, crazy plans for the next interface" and would have "something new" for customers by "early next year." On X he said he looked forward to working with Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, and Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta's Superintelligence Labs.

Conductor was founded in 2024 and launched its core product last summer. Its agentic teams can run in the cloud, locally or from a user's phone, and are designed to let software engineers work on separate parts of a project at the same time. The agents come from major labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI rather than being developed in-house.

For current users, Holtz said Conductor's core features will keep working as they have until early next year. The exception is the cloud service, which will shut down on November 20, after which the company will begin deleting user cloud data.

TechCrunch said Meta, which previously lagged in AI services, has spent recent months trying to catch up. It launched its own coding agent, Muse Code, in August, and said its Muse agents have passed 10 million users. Meta has also made several AI-related acquisitions over the past year, including Moltbook.

Researchers at the security firm Sekoia said on Wednesday that hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws in an attempt to hack visitors to multiple websites, according to Ars Technica. The researchers assessed with "moderate to high confidence" that the attackers were part of Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service. Many of the sites targeted had links to Russia's war against Ukraine.

The attacks began when an iPhone or Android user visited one of potentially hundreds of sites. Injected JavaScript profiled the device, and payloads tailored to the platform tried to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data. The hackers used three routes: direct injection into traffic from legitimate sites, proxy domains, and a supply-chain compromise of a Ukrainian web analytics service that serves thousands of websites. Compromised sites included a top Ukrainian gas production company.

One impersonated site was america250.org, which belongs to a non-partisan group marking the 250th anniversary of the signing of the US Constitution. Another copied the website of Raffles London at The OWO, a hotel near the Ministry of Defence and 10 Downing Street. Sekoia said the choices may have been aimed at invitation-themed spear-phishing or at diplomatic delegations and high-profile guests.

Sekoia said it based its attribution on the targets' profiles and similarities to an earlier attack attributed to APT29. The attacks used three zero-click exploit chains. One was DarkSword, an iOS exploit kit that Google researchers said customers of the Turkish surveillance vendor PARS Defense and at least two other threat actors have used. All the vulnerabilities had already been patched, so the attacks worked only on outdated versions of iOS or Android.

Ukraine's national police released bodycam footage on Wednesday that they say shows the moments between two Russian bomb strikes on the southern village of Kamyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region, according to the BBC. The footage came from a police officer who was killed. It shows residents being told to go to an underground shelter before it was hit. BBC Verify confirmed the video was filmed in the same place as footage of the aftermath released by Ukraine's emergencies service.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said the death toll has risen to 40 and that more than 30 people may still be under the rubble, as the search entered a third day. Local officials had earlier confirmed 37 deaths, Al Jazeera reported. Ukraine said nine glide bombs hit as people gathered for humanitarian aid, and that the shelter was then struck. Four police officers and two rescuers were among the dead. Local authorities said Russian drones were hampering the search but that operations would continue. The Russian military has not publicly commented.
The UN human rights mission in Ukraine said on Tuesday the bombing likely violated international law. Zelensky called it a war crime and said there had been very little reaction from the world.

The attack came before US-brokered talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US set for November 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi. Zelensky said he spoke for an hour and a half with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The BBC said analysts expect no major breakthrough, and Al Jazeera noted earlier rounds produced little progress.

Ethiopia has ordered six Sudanese diplomats to leave within 48 hours and closed Sudan's consulate in the border town of Asosa, according to Ethiopian and Sudanese officials cited by Al Jazeera. The orders came on Tuesday as tensions between the two countries rise, and the title of the report describes the expulsions as tit-for-tat.

Sudan accuses the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group of using Ethiopian territory to launch drone attacks on civilian infrastructure. On Sunday, Sudan lodged complaints with the UN Security Council and the African Union's Peace and Security Council. Addis Ababa denies supporting the RSF, which has been fighting Sudan's military in a civil war since April 2023. Ethiopia, for its part, accuses Sudan's military of backing rebels linked to the Tigray People's Liberation Front, a charge Khartoum denies.

Amjad Farid, a foreign affairs adviser to Sudan's Transitional Sovereign Council, said Sudan remains committed to its right to defend its territory but is making every effort to avoid open war with Ethiopia. Al Jazeera noted that a direct confrontation would strain a Sudanese military that is still fighting the RSF in the southeast.

Ethiopia has also accused Egypt and Eritrea of supporting Tigrayan rebels who launched an offensive against government forces in September. All three countries have rejected the accusations. The latest expulsions follow Ethiopia's decision on October 1 to expel 10 Eritrean diplomats and close its embassy in Eritrea, after which Eritrea severed diplomatic ties. Ethiopia also expelled an Egyptian diplomat last month. Egypt's dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam has long strained relations.

The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates on Thursday, which would be its first increase in more than three years, according to the BBC. Most analysts predict a quarter-point rise from 3.75% to 4%. The announcement is due at 12:00 GMT. The Bank last raised rates in August 2023, and its Monetary Policy Committee has held rates at its last six meetings.

Analysts quoted by the BBC say rising inflation, driven mainly by petrol and diesel costs, will push policymakers toward a hike. Consumer price inflation was 3.5% in the year to September 2026, up from 3.1% the month before and well above the 2% target. The BBC links the pressure to the Iran war's effect on energy and fuel prices. Chris Cheverall of CMC Markets said the Bank must balance inflation that is still too high against a sharply weaker growth outlook, and that attention is shifting to what follows 4%.

A rise would affect borrowers immediately on tracker mortgages. UK Finance calculated that a quarter-point increase would add about £31 a month for a typical tracker holder and about £14 for those on variable deals. Fixed-rate borrowers are not affected right away, and lenders have already priced in the expected rise. Moneyfacts put the average two-year fixed rate at 5.96% and the five-year at 5.99%. Savers could see better rates.

Sterling has also strengthened ahead of the decision. The BBC reported that a Bank of England index of the pound against 18 currencies reached 86.4, joint highest since the June 2016 Brexit referendum, with the Bank due to confirm the figure on Thursday.

David Jones, Australia's upmarket department store, has collapsed into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk, The Guardian reported. Staff were told on Thursday that the board had appointed voluntary administrators from McGrathNicol. The retailer's main financier then installed FTI Consulting as receivers. Under the dual appointment, FTI will take day-to-day control of operations while it restructures the business.

The Guardian said the collapse follows years of steep losses and underperforming stores that left the 188-year-old retailer behind on rent. It came after negotiations broke down with its primary landlord, Scentre Group, the owner of Westfield. Scentre said on Wednesday that David Jones had not paid rent since September. It said it had made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital that would have allowed David Jones to keep trading, and that Anchorage had rejected it. Anchorage bought the retailer from South Africa's Woolworths in 2023 and has now lost operational control.

David Jones employs more than 6,000 staff across 38 stores. The Guardian said the process will almost certainly trigger immediate store closures, though receivers will try to keep the core network open while seeking fresh capital. Analysts expect outer-suburban and regional mall locations to be hit hardest, likely sparing the main city-centre flagships.

Unsecured creditors could face substantial losses, according to the report. Those most at risk include unpaid product suppliers, some of which had already begun redirecting stock to their own outlets, and shoppers holding unredeemed gift vouchers. It is the first time the retailer has been in administration.
